div.p: Mining firms in emerging markets succeed when they also overcome several urgent global issues. For example, they confront environmental impacts, social inequalities and economic uncertainties in regions with limited infrastructure. Mining firms grapple with addressing two urgent ecological crises, climate change and biodiversity loss, in the current Anthropocene era. This is especially so because of the devastating environmental impacts of mining processes. In developed countries, managing disasters resulting from global warming, including heat waves, droughts, floods, and pandemics is largely the responsibility of governments. However, in emerging markets the mining industry plays a more critical role in addressing these challenges, such that it has become an expectation even from the governments, communities and other stakeholders. It has, therefore, become crucial for the industry to actively build resilient host communities that are better prepared to handle the dual crises. Despite social innovation bearing promise as a mechanism for creating community resilience, few studies have analysed how ecological challenges and monitoring of community needs shape social innovation processes. We critically examine how mining companies design interventions to build community resilience and encourage social learning. Our analysis synthesises findings from both resilience studies and social innovation research. We argue that local resources and capabilities, governance and networks, and process dynamism are crucial elements in social innovation processes. They are important in creating resilient communities to deal with ecological shocks and stresses. We further examine how monitoring, evaluation and social learning, together with community attributes, shape social innovation processes and strengthen resilience. We conducted a systematic literature review to develop a framework of social innovation for building resilient mining communities in emerging markets. We end by proposing opportunities for future research to refine our knowledge further and strengthen the ability of mining operations to build resilient communities.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: "The increasing evidence globally of physical climate impactswildfires, floods, rising temperaturesis driving a greater sense of urgency in building adaptive capacity and resilience to climate." (Impala Platinum Limited) The United Nations Sustainable Development Goals 2030 have ecological underpinnings at their core. The central role of ecological imperatives is clearer when we consider that sustainability is defined as development that meets the needs of the present generations without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs (Ramadani et al., 2022;Marco-Lajara, Zaragoza-Sáez, Martínez-Falcó, and Sánchez-García, 2022). Although different interpretations of sustainability have emerged the importance of the environment and how it is impacted by human activities remain unmistakable (Haskell, Bonnedahl and Stål, 2021;Ramadani et al., 2022). Biodiversity is important in fulfilling natural life-support functions like carbon sequestration and withstanding shocks (Kabeyi and Olanrewaju, 2022;Sinha and Baten, 2021) yet the planet has witnessed unprecedented pace and scale of animal and plant species extinction in recent times (Dal Corso et al., 2022). Because of the centrality of human activities on climate and biodiversity, there is a need for initiatives centred on human behaviour to curb ecological crises. Social innovation, defined as new social-centred ways and practices to tackle challenges for improved results, has been proposed as a panacea to ecological crises (e.g., Haskell et al., 2021).

The mining industry plays a critical role in shaping the trajectory of sustainability by linking climate and biodiversity through, for example, deforestation, ocean acidification, and habitat loss caused by expanding mining activity and other related downstream human infrastructure development (Dethier et al., 2023). In South Africa, studies have demonstrated the impacts of mining on the environment. In South Africa, for example, Pretty and Odeku (2017) found that harmful mining activities have negative environmental impacts and significant effects in mining communities. Some scholars have found that loading and hauling make the largest contributions to the total greenhouse gas emissions for the mining and processing of iron ore and bauxite (Norgate and Haque, 2010), creating conditions that worsen global warming (Bennett et al., 2023;Farjana, Huda, Mahmud, and Saidur, 2019). Reversing global warming effects demands an energy transition where the mining industry will play a leading role in supplying the transition technology minerals. However, the rate and magnitude of mineral extraction needed for the energy transition may accelerate ecological crises in mining communities, exposing hosts to the devastating impacts of ecological crises (Farjana et al., op cit). Considering the important role of mining in local sustainability in Southern Africa, finding innovative ways to create community resilience in mining ecosystems is extremely important (Delevingne, Glazener, Grégoir, and Henderson, 2020;Rela, Awang, Ramli, Md Sum, and Meisanti, 2020).

A small but growing body of literature borrows from natural sciences (e.g. Davidson, 2015;Tariq, Pathirage and Fernando, 2021) and ecology (e.g. Cowles et al., 2021;Choudhury, Haque, Nishat and Byrne, 2021) to propose community resilience as an important mechanism to build capacity for communities to not only withstand shocks caused by disasters but transform in preparation for further eventualities (Rifat, and Liu, 2020). Despite the emerging body of work (Haskell et al., 2021) it is argued that extant literature is fragmented, with some scholars focusing on community resilience (e.g., Rifat, and Liu, 2020), while others look at social innovation separately (e.g., Liu, Chen, Zhou, Tang, and Li, 2021). The potential for social innovation in reversing ecological crises is apparent (Hewitt et al., 2019) yet its link with environmental impacts is missing in literature (Olsson et al., 2017;Eichler and Schwarz, 2019;Castro-Arce, and Vanclay, 2020). This surprising omission underscores the shortcomings of social innovation literature in integrating deep social change needed to build strong sustainable resilience in mining communities. In the context of a mining industry undergoing modernisation, we take a broader definition of innovation to mean not merely industrial, but rather a means to actualise society's capacity to organize, act and respond to the persisting challenges of growth, and capitalise on the knowledge generation and transfer opportunities provided by new technology (Angelidou and Psaltoglou, 2017). This paper draws on resilience studies to clarify how social innovation can deliver sustainable development outcomes. Integrating these two bodies of literature in the context of sustainable development in South Africa generates a significant contribution to theory. Examining social innovation and community resilience in mining regions offers potential to generate fresh theoretical insights. Morris, Aguilera, Fisher, and Thatcher (2023) argue that the settings of emerging markets have huge opportunities for incubating new theories. In locating the review in sustainable development logic, the paper introduces measuring, evaluating, and learning in building a dynamic model of social innovation to enhance resilience in mining communities.

From a practical perspective, the paper addresses ecological crises, which is an important topic for the mining industry at a time when there are calls for accelerated mineral extraction in the face of the need to reverse the effects of global warming through an energy transition (Gielen, 2021). The mining industry has been identified as playing a leading role in the just energy transition (Dou, Xu and Keenan, 2023;Srivastava and Kumar, 2022), yet there are growing fears that the accelerated exploitation of critical minerals could worsen human rights violations, ecological impacts, and fuel conflicts in host communities (Church and Crawford, 2020;Srivastava, 2023;Buhmann, 2023). In addition to the widely celebrated technological innovation the industry is going through (Chipangamate et al., 2023), there is a need to keep in mind how social innovation could accelerate sustainable development in mining ecosystems (Sauer and Hiete, 2019). The paper contributes to theory and practice by answering the following questions: 1) How is social innovation conceptualised in the context of global south mining host communities? 2) How and under what conditions does social innovation play a role in creating mining host community resilience? 3) What would a model of social innovation look like in the context of sustainable development in mining communities in the era of climate change?

div.head: Methods
div.p: We undertook a systematic literature review to integrate existing knowledge on social innovation and resilience. The method was relevant here because the literature on social innovation is growing and calls for a variety of approaches (Okoli, 2015). A literature review allowed us to narrow the literature linking social innovation to the environment, nature, and society. Thus, we examined this segment of the literature by extracting, analysing, and assessing how it portrayed social innovation and aligned it with strong sustainability, and community resilience. To assess social innovation in reviewed articles, we mobilised a framework developed by Howaldt et al. (2014;2017), which has been extensively used in the past for empirical analyses of hundreds of social innovations (Edwards-Schachter and Wallace, 2017;Phillips et al., 2015;Silveira and Zilber, 2017).

div.head: Conceptualising social innovation
div.p: The world is grappling with the dual ecological crises of climate change and loss in biodiversity which have had debilitating effects on society (Haskell et al., 2021). For example, incessant droughts, floods, and heat waves have taken a toll on livelihoods in different parts of the world (Zakari, Tawiah, Khan, Alvarado, and Li, 2022;Haskell et al., 2021). What seems to be clear is the realisation that the world needs a radical social change, focusing on today's social practices and ways of organizing to challenge dominant norms and beliefs (Wittmayer, Backhaus, Avelino, Pel, Strasser, Kunze and Zuijderwijk, 2019;Pel et al., 2020;Heikkurinen, Young and Morgan, 2019) in line with a strong version of resilience (Rifat, and Liu, 2020). The need for deep social change is further compounded by the failure of market-based solutions, new technologies, and regulations to remedy today's human-caused ecological crises (Gao, Xu, Hou, and Ouyang, 2020;UNEP, 2021).

Community resilience from strong sustainability implies that critical environmental capacities and qualities cannot be substituted, but rather sustained, as prerequisites for social and economic activities and functions (Stål, 2018). The strong sustainability perspective is to be contrasted with weak sustainable resilience which aligns with current norms and beliefs. Weak sustainability includes the view that trade-offs between three dimensions of sustainability, that is, social, economic, and environmental, are both possible and required (e.g., United Nations, 2015; Bonnedahl and Caramujo, 2018).

Social innovation refers to new combinations of practices in social action that address needs more effectively than established approaches (Howaldt and Butzin, 2014;Haskell et al., 2021). To be transformative (Avelino et al., 2017), social innovation needs to challenge and change dominant institutions within specific contexts, and alter social relations (Pel et al., 2020). It is important to note that the approaches to contemporary ecological crises provided by social innovation differ from traditional technology-based solutions such as reduced emissions through new fuels (Bonnedahl, 2021;Bonnedahl and Caramujo, 2018). The novel approaches demonstrate relevance for sustainable lifestyle changes (Mont et al., 2014) and may provide the springboard for sustainable start-ups (Piccarozzi, 2017). There is, therefore, a need for a genuine relook into the ways and possibilities that exist in how society relates with the environment for building resilience. This contrasts with the superficial focus on shifts in markets and regulations, which is a necessary but insufficient condition to build resilience. Further research to understand social innovation is necessary because the current focus of weak sustainable resilience could be attributable to conceptual ambiguity and literature fragmentation (Edwards-Schachter and Wallace, 2017;Grimm et al., 2013), which limits depiction of social innovation as deep social transformations. As Haskell et al. (2021) observe, social innovation is often promoted by governments and municipalities with ambitions that may better be described as support for insufficient or failing public services and systems. The same could be said of the mining industry in Southern Africa, which is expected to play an important role in driving sustainable development (Chipangamate et al., 2023).

There are still alternative depictions of social innovations conceptualising them as new non-market initiatives, which harness crosssectoral collaboration and citizen empowerment to improve societal capacities and fairer resource use (Caulier-Grice et al., 2012;Murray et al., 2010). To give examples, citizens are combating global issues within their contexts, through local sharing economy initiatives, local food production, and ecosystem safeguarding initiatives (Schartinger et al., 2017). In South Africa, an example of social innovation is Impact Catalyst, which is an initiative founded by Anglo American, the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), Exxaro, and World Vision South Africa, to create mechanisms that drive large-scale, initiatives for socio-economic development through public-private partnerships in mining communities. The initiatives are designed to leverage collaboration across all sectors and selected for impact beyond the scale of individual participants. We argue that the diffusion of such initiatives demonstrates social innovation's transformative power to change societal structures: institutions, cultural patterns, and social practices (Howaldt, 2017;Pel et al., 2020;Sauer, and Hiete, 2019). Together, the definitions presented in Table 1 speak to the diversity of approaches to social innovation, with varying level of relevance for strong sustainable resilience in mining communities. They represent some of the widely used definitions of social innovation in extant literature.

Having looked at the definitions of social innovation, next we consider the framing of the concept and practice. A framework comprehensive enough to assess this relevance was found in one developed by Howaldt et al. (2014;2017). This framework was deemed comprehensive as it combines innovation studies and theories of social change and focuses on social practices and innovation orientated towards major societal challenges (Howaldt et al., 2014;Howaldt and Hochgerner, 2017). It has been applied in relation to environmental challenges (Schartinger et al., 2017 andHaskell et al., 2021) and therefore, proven useful in empirical analyses. The framework identified five key dimensions of social innovation as a) environmental needs and challenges (in this paper, we use ecological needs and challenges to include climate change and biodiversity), b) sound concept and understanding of social innovation, c) resources, capabilities, constraints, d) governance, networks, actors, and e) process dynamics. Because the paper is leveraging social innovation for community resilience, we also borrow insights from the theory of community resilience. Fig. 1 shows the five dimensions of social innovation.
This section has attempted to conceptualise social innovation. The next section focuses on community resilience to critically review literature relevant in the context of social innovation.

div.head: Community resilience
div.p: Resilience has been defined in multiple ways across natural science and social science disciplines. For example, 'resilience' is fundamentally a metaphor applied in theorisation of the relationship between people and their environments. That conceptualisation finds roots in the sciences of physics and mathematics, where the term was originally used to describe the capacity of a material or system to return to equilibrium after a displacement (Nikinmaa, Lindner, Cantarello, Jump, Seidl, Winkel and Muys, 2020). Borrowing the concept from natural sciences, Holling (1973) in his original and influential thesis about ''ecological resilience'' was able to invoke vivid imagination of ecological processes. Since then, the concept has had wide usage to describe the adaptive capacities of individuals, human communities, and larger societies (Strier, 2021).

Besides having a metaphorical origin, the concept of resilience has developed to the level of theory. In the context of mining communities, it emphasises the capacity for successful adaptation in the face of disturbance, stress, or adversity (Van Meerbeek, Jucker and Svenning, 2021). Studies that take this perspective distinguish resistance, defined in mathematics and technology terms as the force required to displace the system from equilibrium, whereas resilience refers to the time required for the system to return to equilibrium once displaced (Abd Majid, Mohd Zahari, Jipiu, Kutut and Bashir, 2022). Table 2 is a collection of some of the widely used definitions of resilience in literature. From the wide spectrum of definitions, two important themes standout: a) resilience is more of a process rather than an outcome (Calderón-Contreras and White, 2020), b) resilience is dynamic than static (Ruiz-Ballesteros and Ramos-Ballesteros, 2019). Therefore, resilience is a dynamic process linking a set of adaptive capacities to a positive trajectory of functioning and adaptation after a disturbance. Building on Norris et al. (2008) and Partelow (2021) theorisation, we utilise their four dimensions of resilience a) economic development, b) social capitals, c) information and communication, and d) community capacity, to build a theory of social innovation. We briefly define these dimensions in the following passages:

div.head: Economic development
div.p: Economic development is a measure of two elements a) resource volumes and diversity within communities (encompassing economic growth, adaptability of livelihoods, and equitable distribution of income and assets within populations, land and raw materials, physical capital, accessible housing, health services, schools, and employment opportunities). The use of complementary currencies to strengthen community resilience by countering fragility and resource-intensity in production and consumption systems will be useful (Liu, Cao, Yang and Anderson, 2022). Extreme events, such as droughts, floods, or infestations increase the risk of being dependent on resources and therefore decrease resilience (Partelow, 2021), b) Resource equity and social vulnerability suggests that societies do not equitably allocate the risks of climate change and biodiversity loss, such that the poorest communities become the weakest links in hazard mitigation (Liu et al., 2022). This is evident within local communities, but also among developed and developing economies.

Mining organisations play a critical role in fostering economic development in mining host communities. For example, in South Africa and Zimbabwe, Impala Platinum Holdings Limited (Implats) is doing so by establishing a long-term strategic focus to help community enterprises become part of their supply chain and to transition to provide their services beyond their local ecosystem. This is under the rubric of enterprise and supplier development (ESD) initiatives in South Africa and local economic development (LED) initiatives in Zimbabwe (Implats, 2022).

div.head: Social capital
div.p: The central principle of social capital is that individuals invest, access, and use resources embedded in social networks to gain emotional, material, tangible or informational benefits (Liu et al., 2022). From this conceptualisation, social capital represents the aggregate of actual or potential resources that are linked to individuals possessing a durable network of relationships. The first important element of social capital are network structures and linkages, which are important in creating community capacity. Community capacity is defined as the presence of inter-group networks that are characterized by reciprocal links, frequent supportive interactions, overlap with other networks, the ability to form new associations, and cooperative decision-making processes (Shahnewaz, 2021). It is important to note, however, that the presence of hubs in networks could be a source of vulnerability in the event of the hub collapsing (Carmen et al., 2022). The second important element of social capital is social support. Social support refers to social interactions that provide individuals with actual assistance and embed them into a web of social relationships perceived to be loving, caring, and readily available in times of need. The two important dimensions of support are the source (where the support comes from such as friends, relatives, local NGOs, or mining company), the second is type of support (which can be emotional, material, tangible or informational). Social support is closely linked to social influence, such that in the event of need for evacuation, for example, people with stronger social support are more likely to find the help needed in disasters (Liu et al., 2022). The third important elements are the community bonds, roots, and commitment, which refers to how building a sense of community is very important in resilient communities for enabling an attitude of bonding (trust and belonging) with other members of one's group or locale (González-Anta, Orengo, Zornoza, Peñarroja and Martínez-Tur, 2021; Cheng, Gu and Mou, 2020). Community bonds, roots and commitment are created when people have attachment to a place, which is a sense of belonging to a place in addition to the specific people in the area (Cheng, Gu and Mou, 2020). In addition to these attributes, an important element is ''citizen participation'', which is the engagement of community members in formal organizations, including religious congregations, school and resident associations, neighbourhood watches, and self-help groups (González-Anta, Orengo, Zornoza, Peñarroja and Martínez-Tur, 2021).

div.head: Community competence
div.p: Literature demonstrates that communities faced with challenges could be improved when they are able to learn about their risks and options and work together flexibly and creatively to solve problems (Adekola and Clelland, 2020). Literature has emphasised importance of the capacity to acquire trusted and accurate information, to reflect on that information critically, and solve emerging problems as far more important for community resilience than is a detailed security plan that rarely foresees all contingencies (Chen, Das and Ivanov, 2019). Community competence is about how people work together to make decisions and act, which depends on their belief in their collective ability and the empowerment gained from participating in community activities (Adekola and Clelland, 2020). The idea is to have shared rights and responsibility for resource management and decentralization of decision making for common good, which are best suited to promoting resilience (Albareda and Sison, 2020).

However, since we are specifically focusing on community as the level of analysis, a further complexity to understanding community resilience emerges from the lack of clarity in conceptualising community. Very few scholars define the concept of community. We define a community as an entity that has geographic boundaries and shared fate (Bacq, Hertel and Lumpkin, 2022). Communities are composed of built, natural, social, and economic environments (giving it identity) that influence one another in complex ways, such that community resilience implies the joint resilience of the whole not individual actors (Valeri and Baggio, 2021). From this definition, three important aspects of community are discernible, a) community of geography (Bacq, Hertel and Lumpkin, 2022), b) community of interest (Axon, 2020), and c) community identity (Hertel, Bacq and Belz, 2019;Bacq, Hertel and Lumpkin, 2022).

We adopted McFarlane and Norris' (2006) definition of disaster as ''a potentially traumatic event that is collectively experienced, has an acute onset, and is time delimited. Disasters may be attributed to natural, technological, or human causes (Kusumasari & Prabowo, 2020; Tavares, Luís, Henriques, Marujo, Gonçalves and Rivero, 2023). This definition includes acts of nature, such as hurricanes, floods, and earthquakes; large industrial, transportation, and nuclear accidents; and episodes of mass violence, such as terrorist attacks and shooting sprees. It excludes chronic environmental hazards, ongoing community and political violence, war, and epidemics.

div.head: Towards a dynamic social innovation framework for creating community resilience (CCR)
Social innovation and creating community resilience (CCR)
Understanding societal needs and ecological challenges to create community resilience
div.p: Literature on social innovation has identified societal needs and challenges as an important consideration for advancing societal growth and advancement (Eichler and Schwarz, 2019). A growing need for environmental conservation has been discussed in several studies aligned with strong sustainability (e.g., Hewitt et al., 2019;Prokopy et al., 2019). For example, Song, Song, Gu & Li (2020) focused on pollution in mining contexts, and some scholars have discussed the urgent challenges accompanying the Anthropocene, such as climate change and biodiversity loss (e.g., Olsson et al., 2017). The focus of literature has been on environmental conservation through forest ecosystem management (Hewitt et al., 2019;Prokopy et al., 2019).

The effects of climate change on social wellbeing in mining communities is well documented (e.g., Olsson et al., 2017;Saedpanah and Amanollahi, 2019;Tian, Liang and Li, 2019). Tian, Liang & Li (2019) argue that fine road dust contamination in a mining area presents a likely air pollution hotspot and threat to human health, whereas Zhang and Wang (2020) observe the detrimental effects of mining due to heavy metal soil pollution. Similarly, the need to contain emissions has become urgent in mining ecosystems, with scholars proposing remote sensing and deployment of other technologies to monitor pollution (Song, Song, Gu and Li, 2020). In addition to monitoring pollution, mining organisations are expected by stakeholders to address social needs and recurrent challenges faced in mining communities to foster strong sustainable development (Hewitt et al., 2019;Prokopy et al., 2019), support forest-dependent mining communities and prevent tourism-mining conflicts (Sisneros-Kidd, Monz, Hausner, Schmidt and Clark, 2019). Mining operations are called upon to address consumption and livelihoods challenges, such as displacements to pave way for solar and wind farms associated with mining activities (Kramarz, Park and Johnson, 2021), and water problems caused by underground extraction, such as in lithium mining and processing. The technology used in brine extraction has been reported to create underground water shortages in mining communities in Chile (Alessia, Alessandro, Maria, Carlos and Francesca, 2021; Liu, Agusdinata and Myint, 2019; Kaunda, 2020). Similarly, underground water is pumped in drought prone Masvingo and Matabeleland regions in Zimbabwe for lithium processing. This has resulted in underground water shortages for communities. Social innovation has been suggested as a plausible solution for specific local environmental issues (Haskell et al., 2021), and for urgent interlinked global challenges with local impacts (Olsson et al., 2017).

A growing body of literature suggests that increasing industrialization, expanding urbanization, and decaying infrastructures will lead to an escalation in the frequency and severity of ecological disasters worldwide and that developing countries will bear the brunt of this trend (Radović and Iglesias, 2019). Considering that in developing countries' rural areas housing quality is poor, it is likely that the impacts of climate disasters will be more severe. This situation is worsened by lack of the means for obtaining alternative shelter in the event of disasters (Ling et al., 2022;Giri, Bista, Singh and Pandey, 2021) and the poor fiscal policies to deal with such disasters (Catalano, Forni and Pezzolla, 2020). In the mining communities in the East Coast of South Africa and in Madagascar, ecological disasters have been worsened by the nature of mining operations which destroy sand dunes (Nurzaman, Shaw and Roychansyah, 2020;Werner, Bebbington and Gregory, 2019) and build tailings facilities which may be susceptible to flooding or failure and climate change impacts worsen (Lyu, Chai, Xu, Qin and Cao, 2019;Mebratu-Tsegaye, Toledano, Dietrich Brauch and Greenberg, 2021). More recently, in Madagascar, mining operation tailings dam materials were released into nearby rivers leading to deaths of fish and a moratorium to fishing, which deprived local communities of important livelihoods (Orego, 2022). This followed the risk of tailings facility collapsing following heavy rain induced flooding, which resulted in the mining company and the government voluntarily releasing pollutants into the environment (Orego, op cit).

It is also important to note that developing societies often face challenges in mobilising resources in the event of a disaster. As other scholars have stated, the mobilisation and distribution of post disaster support should ideally follow the ''rule of relative needs'' (the most support goes to those who need it the most), yet the distribution of support follows the ''rule of relative advantage'' because one's embeddedness in the community, political connections, and social class determine the availability and accessibility of resources (Kaniasty, 2020). This has significant implications for mining companies mobilising resources in disaster situations.

From the several definitions and conceptualisations identified in the paper (see Table 2), there has not been consensus in setting boundaries for the social innovation concept (Howaldt and Hochgerner, 2017). A common thread, though, in various definitions is viewing social innovation as initiatives that profoundly change basic routines and beliefs within a social system (Howaldt and Butzin, 2014). However, in terms of the focus, scholars have tended to differ in terms of geographical coverage. For example, in some cases, change is understood as happening within local contexts (McCarthy et al., 2014 andBiggs et al., 2010), whereas, conversely, Olsson et al. (2017) viewed profound change as a macro-level phenomenon affecting society at large. Although literature has attempted to addresses the global twin challenges of biodiversity loss and climate change, for creating community resilience, the focus has been at the local level (McCarthy et al., 2014 andBiggs et al., 2010). Some scholars have seen social innovation (Liu et al., 2022;McCarthy et al., 2022) and community resilience (Chen, Das and Ivanov, 2019;Carmen et al., 2022) as outcomes, whereas some have viewed the two as ongoing processes of capacity creation (Grimm et al., 2013;Eichler and Schwarz, 2019;Haskell et al., 2021). Further, resilience literature has several streams such as ecological resilience (Calderón-Contreras and White, 2020), economic resilience (Abd Majid et al., 2022) and cultural resilience (Chen, Xie and Liu, 2021). In this paper we looked at strong sustainable resilience which focuses on all the three dimensions of resilience under the variable 'creating community resilience' (CCR) (Liu et al., 2022).

To build resilient mining host communities, for example, Impala Platinum Holdings Limited (Implats), realising the challenging socioeconomic contexts in which they operate, particularly in South Africa and Zimbabwe, highlighted the need for sustainable community development as a commercial and social imperative. It is important to note that mining companies in these countries are obligated by legal and policy frameworks to mine responsibly. In Zimbabwe, the Environmental management Act (EMA), enacted in 2002, aims to promote sustainable environmental management and protect natural resources. The Act establishes a framework for environmental assessment, regulating activities that may impact the environment, and ensuring compliance with environmental standards. It also emphasizes public participation in environmental decision-making and the need for education and awareness regarding environmental issues. The EMA is crucial for addressing challenges such as deforestation, pollution, and land degradation, promoting conservation efforts, and fostering sustainable development in the country.

Similarly, the National Environmental Management Act (NEMA) of South Africa, enacted in 1998, serves as the cornerstone of the country's environmental legislation. It aims to promote sustainable development by providing a framework for environmental governance and management. NEMA establishes principles for decision-making, emphasizes public participation, and outlines procedures for environmental impact assessments (EIAs) for mining projects that may affect the environment. The Act also addresses issues such as biodiversity conservation, pollution control, and the protection of ecosystems, aiming to balance economic growth with environmental sustainability. Overall, NEMA plays a critical role in promoting environmental justice and ensuring the responsible use of natural resources in South Africa. Governments should not only enact legislation but also demonstrate active accountability through independent audits, public reporting of enforcement actions and inclusive stakeholder consultations. Such measures will ensure that existing laws translate into real-world protection for mining communities (Rajah, Jerie and Rajah, 2012;Tshehla and Wright, 2019).

Typically, mining operations in developing and emerging markets represent a centre of socio-economic activity and an important source of welfare because the operations are in rural areas characterised by limited formal economic activity, high levels of youth unemployment, inadequate provision of infrastructure and poor service delivery. For example, in South Africa's uMfolozi Local Municipality, an area close to mineral sands mining operations in the eastern coast, the unemployment rate is 42 %, while youth unemployment is 50.4 % and the dependency ratio is 68.2 % (uMfolozi Local Municipality, 2023). Socially innovative interventions are, therefore, designed by mining companies to ensure that in the event of disasters induced by climate change the communities are resilient.

A typical example of how mining organisations utilise their capabilities to address climate change challenges is Rio Tinto in Madagascar. QIT Madagascar Minerals (QMM) produces ilmenite near Fort Dauphin, Madagascar, which is essential for titanium dioxide used in paints and paper. The mine views water as crucial for local communities and environmental stability, making effective water management a priority. In 2023, QMM developed an AI tool to forecast rainfall up to six months in advance, allowing for better tracking of climate influences and improved planning for operations during the variable wet season (Rio Tinto, 2025). On their risk profile, Rio Tinto (op cit) stated that flooding could lead to failures in tailings storage facilities due to instability and erosion, causing underground and surface pits to flood. Water stress and drought may also compromise tailings facilities and lead to similar flooding issues. On the other hand, heat extremes can increase health and safety risks for the workforce and communities while reducing productivity. Wildfires pose safety risks to both workers and nearby communities, potentially damaging mining and community infrastructure and disrupting operations and supply chains. Similarly, tropical cyclones present similar threats, with risks of wind and flood damage to equipment and infrastructure. Additionally, coastal extremes can inundate infrastructure, disrupt operations, and increase flooding risks for coastal communities.

Rio Tinto has developed the Climate Change Resilience Assessment Methodology (CCRA) to evaluate how climate change may affect their tailings storage facilities. The CCRA involves assessing critical elements like drains and slopes, comparing current designs against future climate scenarios, identifying potential risks and their impacts, and formulating plans to further evaluate and mitigate risks for any vulnerable features. This comprehensive methodology helps ensure the resilience of operations in the face of changing climate conditions. A company contributes to community resilience when it shares climate change data with local stakeholders, enabling informed decision making and collective adaptation.

These observations demonstrate an important consideration and relevant for this paper which is the emphasis in literature of the need for context specific conceptualisation of social innovation in areas such as social entrepreneurship or inclusive innovation, which is gaining influence in the context of developing economies (e.g., Cheng et al., 2020;Hertel et al., 2019). Based on these arguments the following is suggested: Proposition 1. Mining operations' engagement in identifying and understanding community needs and ecological-driven crises should generate innovation that comes from using resources and capabilities, which contributes to resilience.

div.head: Resources, capabilities, constraints and CCR
div.p: Studies have demonstrated that resources are an important consideration for social innovation. For example, in a review of social innovation literature, Haskell at al. (2021) find that human resources were mentioned throughout the articles that aligned with strong sustainability as a key resource for successful social innovation. The authors argue that stakeholder engagement, citizen participation, citizen empowerment, encouraging collaboration (Biggs et al., 2010;Chatfield and Reddick, 2016;McCarthy et al., 2014), and activism (Castro-Arce et al., 2019) are important categories of social innovation. However, for these categories to be more effective when social innovation is aimed at creating community resilience, empowerment of people directly experiencing the ecological challenges and who need change was identified as an important human resource mechanism for mobilising people to deal with challenges (Chatfield and Reddick, 2016;McCarthy et al., 2014r). Empowerment can reinforce social innovation, as demonstrated by Angelidou and Psaltoglou (2017) who showed the importance of involving those that benefitted from a social innovation to induce change. Kabeyi and Olanrewaju (2022) exemplified how citizen participation increased the use of renewable energy which is an important aspect of ecological adaptation and resilience. Another area through which mining operations are leveraging human resources is by having dedicated committees that deal with biodiversity and climate change. For example, Implats and several other mining companies have established the Health, Safety, and Environment Committee (HSECom) to oversee governance, monitoring, and strategic planning for health, safety, environment, and climate change risks they face. They have integrated climate change considerations into the Committee's activities, and a Group Executive: Sustainability is responsible for climate-related actions (Implats, 2023).

In addition to human resources, financial resources were also found to be important mechanism for achieving social innovation in different contexts including forestry dependent communities (e.g., Nijnik, Secco, Miller and Melnykovych, 2019), renewable energy (Kabeyi and Olanrewaju, 2022), and environmental conservation (e.g., Biggs et al., 2010;Castro-Arce et al., 2019;McCarthy et al., 2014). Funding could be deployed as social innovation coming from government (Soma et al., 2018), private investment, a combination of government and private fund in public-private partnerships (Hekkel et al., 2021), or from active users through sustainable consumption such as buying second-hand or recycled products (Martin and Upham, 2016). Lack of funding is a major constraint to social innovation's long-term success. For instance, McCarthy et al. (2014) showed how governments could shift funds away from ongoing social innovation through uncoordinated policy. In such instances, enhanced coordination becomes an important social innovation process.

Collaboration is an important mechanism for driving social innovation in communities (Kabeyi and Olanrewaju, 2022). For example, in South Africa, a partnership of the government, mining companies and a not-for-profit organisations, Impact Catalyst and World Vision mobilised resources to finance agricultural activities in mining communities (Impact Catalyst, 2023).

Natural resources are not widely seen as a driver of social innovation, yet Haskell et al. (2021) argue for broadening our understanding of social innovation, as changes in biodiversity and alternative uses of natural resources could be a source of innovation. For example, use of local natural resources for tourism or carbon credits is a new use that may both help conserve the environment and generate income for communities to build resilience (Hajjar, Engbring and Kornhauser, 2021). A typical example of this is the conservation of flora and fauna around Rio Tinto's QMM operation in Madagascar to form part of the local heritage. However, this was faced with community resistance, as communities were deprived of their traditional hunting and fishing livelihoods (Orogo, 2022). This illuminates the important need for meaningful dialogue and genuine stakeholder engagement when mining operations take part in social innovation, considering that ecological crises are characteristically cross-scalar (Haskell et al., 2021). Although human made resources have had limited research, there is evidence these are needed for social innovation. For example, Chatfield and Reddick (2016) identified smart technology as vital, while some authors (e.g., Chatfield, Reddick, Baldwin, Donnellan and Chung, 2019) stressed the role of technology in attaining desirable societal outcomes, including through communication of sustainable consumption (Fischer, Reinermann, Mandujano, DesRoches, Diddi & Vergragt, 2021).

To generate the most from resources, we argue that some conditions are necessary, especially in emerging markets mining communities. These include dynamic capabilities such as bricolage, defined as the ability to recombine existing ideas, practices, and concepts (McCarthy et al., 2014;Olsson et al., 2017). As Olsson et al. (2017) argued bricolage has the potential of helping society to break away from path-dependency, to turn humans into a positive, rather than negative force upon natural ecosystems. This is especially true when bricolage is creatively combined with other key capabilities that can enable the brokering of stakeholder relationships (Biggs et al., 2010;Castro-Arce et al., 2019;McCarthy et al., 2014). An aspect that presents both an opportunity and a constraint in emerging markets is technology. In developed markets, the use of technology has been reported to mobilize citizen participation to help track flooding (Ferri, Wehn, See and Fritz, 2019). If the same strategy is to be deployed in emerging markets where most people may be technologically excluded, a capability that needs developing would be that of sharing technological and other resources (Fischer, Reinermann, Mandujano, DesRoches, Diddi & Vergragt, 2021). This is even more important considering that scholars have identified technology as a key constraint in social innovation. Haskell et al. (2021) argued that the widespread insistence on new technologies, changing governmental priorities, lack of finances, and stakeholder conflicts are the leading challenges facing social innovation today. Thus, mining firms have an opportunity to play a leading role in fostering social innovation, especially in emerging and developing countries. In view of all this, the following proposition is suggested: Proposition 2. The resources and capabilities that contribute to creating community resilience (CCR) are strengthened when mining operations deliberately identify constraints and leverage collaborative bricolage within the host community.

div.head: Governance, networks, actors
div.p: Identification of key actors and existing networks is important for effective social innovation. Some of the actors identified in literature include citizens, industry leaders, and municipality representatives involved in smart city projects (Chatfield and Reddick, 2016), civil society (Castro-Arce et al., 2019), cross-sectoral collaborations and individuals in networks (Haskell et al., 2021). Another consideration when analysing cross-sectoral collaborations is the specific context, which informs the actual actors and their roles. These are necessary in social innovation as a creative change in actors and their roles could be a defining factor in societal outcomes. For this to be effective, stakeholder dialogue is suggested to ensure lasting and successful cross-sectoral collaborations (e.g. Biggs et al., 2010;Chatfield and Reddick, 2016).

Different actors could play significant roles in social innovation including entrepreneurs who can lead change and foster innovation, while civil society actively participate in engagement and environmentalist lead activism initiatives to ignite conservation. Where multiple stakeholders are involved a wide range of governance systems are available to manage relationships. Some of the widely used governance mechanisms are top-down governance, coupled with a shared vision (Castro-Arce et al., 2019), democratic governance (Biggs et al., 2010), and bottom-up citizen-centric governance (Chatfield and Reddick, 2016). The different approaches are adopted according to the context of the mining community. This helps encourage participation and engagement of citizens and grassroots for social innovation and collaborative decision making it involves. All in all, this suggests the following.

Proposition 3. The active participation of mining firms in the community generates influence stemming from their ability to manage governance mechanisms, networks, and other stakeholders, which contributes to creating community resilience.

div.head: Process dynamics
div.p: Following Olsson et al. (2017) we argue for scaling "up, out, and deep", meaning that social innovation does not just need to diffuse (out) within a given context, but need to influence and grow within an institutional setting (up), and shift beliefs, values, and ways of being (deep). For this reason, there is need to reach critical mass to create new social practices by engaging enough citizens and stakeholders to enact necessary behavioural changes at a meaningful scale (Chatfield and Reddick, 2016;Hatkell, et al., 2021). All actors need to combine efforts for scaling social innovations. This calls for dynamic processes to balance the challenge of imitation (where global solutions could be adopted in local communities) and the need for locality (where local solutions were created for local problems) (e.g., Biggs et al., 2010;Castro-Arce et al., 2019) because perfect imitation is not always appropriate. Ecological challenges are global but have local implications. This makes it difficult to scale social micro innovations, which are bound by their local contexts and participants from to macro levels (Haskell et al., 2021).

Alongside imitation, social learning was discussed in articles aligning with strong sustainability. McCarthy et al. (2014) found that leaders and participants leveraged institutional support to learn about their context and each other over time enabling them to adapt a shared vision and continuously maintain long-term relationships. However, social learning will be effective under conditions of community absorptive capacity to learn about vulnerabilities so that implemented solutions lead to impact. Further, it may be necessary that practices and behaviours are institutionalised for social innovation to bring about social change. For example, novel solutions brought forth by social innovation may have institutional outcomes, such as new social practices or new policy (Haskell et al., 2021). Castro-Arce et al. ( 2019) found social innovation to result in transformed governance such as social change regarding how protected areas were governed, stressing changed relationships between local stakeholders that may require a more collaborative governance.

Social innovation may result in behavioural change. For example, Chatfield and Reddick (2016) discovered that as citizens used more smart city technologies, their lifestyles became more environmentally sustainable. Scholars have noted changes in both behaviour and how communities relate with their environment (Castro-Arce et al., 2019). Despite this positive development, scholars have cautioned on potential environmental and human rights violations in host communities due to accelerated mining necessitated by rising demand for renewable energy minerals (see Owen, Kemp, Lechner, Harris, Zhang and Lèbre, 2023;Islam and Murakami, 2021;Boocock, 2002). In emerging markets, sometimes there is need for policy changes to align with the necessitated behavioural changes on the part of society and mining companies (McCarthy et al., 2018). It is suggested that improved policy frameworks could contribute to improved environmental and social performance in mining ecosystems (Liu, Alharthi, Atil, Zafar and Khan, 2022). For example, Rio Tinto revisited their company policies regarding how they relate with their environment, and communities and their heritage, including in emerging markets, following the blowing of an Aboriginal Cave in Pilbara in Australia (Bird, 2022). Therefore, policies need to be dynamic at organisational, local government, national government and broadly at the global stage. Taken together, these arguments and examples suggest the following proposition.

Proposition 4. The active engagement of mining firms in the community generates benefits in form of process dynamism stemming from social learning and deeper behavioural and policy changes, which contribute to creating community resilience.

div.head: Community attributes, social innovation and creating community resilience
div.p: Community attributes refer to the characteristics of the host community context in which the mining company operates. The effectiveness of a community's response to a hazard is shaped by a combination of resources (such as sufficient education to understand the technical issues, money to hire lawyers or scientific advisors), a culture that permits challenges to authority, institutions that provide a basis for coordinating a response, and political mechanisms that involve citizens in decision-making (Raymond et al., 2020). Building on the model by Pareja-Cano, Valor & Benito (2023) we argue this to be a process of empowerment which progresses through formal empowerment (mechanisms for citizen input), intrapersonal empowerment (feelings of personal competence and confidence), instrumental empowerment (ability to participate in and influence decision, as determined by knowledge, material resources, and persuasiveness), and substantive empowerment (ability to reach decisions that solve problems).

In addition to all these, the community's active agency and other physical infrastructure are important for building resilience (Ruiz-Ballesteros and Ramos-Ballesteros, 2019). Some scholars have also identified active participation of communities in cutting carbon emissions and encouraging environmentally friendly agriculture and sustainable economic production systems (Radović and Iglesias, 2019;Zakari et al., 2022). Some important attributes include ability and skills of communities for various activities, including visioning exercises, awareness raising, connecting existing local groups, and leading a range of practical projects such as community agriculture, car clubs, reskilling classes, neighbourhood carbon reduction groups, and local currencies (Watson, Boyle, Mullally and Gallachóir, 2020) to reduce vulnerability to environmental change (Ruiz-Ballesteros et al., 2019).

Together, these attributes form and inform the broader meaning of community competence. Community competence speaks to capacities that manifest in population wellness, defined as high and non-disparate levels of mental and behavioural health, functioning, and quality of life (Nikinmaa et al., 2020;Kimhi, Marciano, Eshel and Adini, 2020;Wickes, Zahnow, Corcoran and Kimpton, 2022;Bhadra, 2023). Collective resilience in communities is built by reducing risk and resource inequities. It is important for mining companies to engage local people in risk mitigation so as to benefit from indigenous knowledge and encourage collaborative social support among communities (Norris et al., 2008). Building on these arguments, it is proposed that:

Proposition 5: The benefits of social innovation stem from understanding the needs and challenges of the community. Mining firms should leverage resources and capabilities, governance, networks and actors, and process dynamism to support communities. It is necessary that communities have active agency, absorptive capacity to learn, collaboration culture, and supporting infrastructure as preconditions to create community resilience.
Fig. 4 shows the linkages among the propositions presented in this paper.

div.head: Social innovation impact assessment-measuring, evaluating, and social learning
div.p: Although there is growing research interest on social resilience in disaster management there is lack of consistency in concepts used to measure social resilience (Chen, Xie and Liu, 2021). Following an extensive review of social resilience assessment frameworks, evidence revealed that important process-oriented indicators are not included in social resilience frameworks, pointing to their dynamic nature which makes it difficult to operationalise (Saja, Teo, Goonetilleke, Ziyath and Nianthi, 2020). This, therefore, underscores the need for developing comprehensive social resilience frameworks that can be adapted to different contexts and integrated with specific tools and guidelines (Chen et al., 2021). For this reason, this paper integrates measuring, evaluating, and learning as important elements of such a model. Some scholars have categorised the methods to measure resilience as quantitative methods (mainly index based measures), qualitative methods such as case studies/life stories/observations, and participatory tools/toolkits (for example, participatory hazard mapping) (Saja, Goonetilleke, Teo and Ziyath, 2019;Eligue, 2023;Le Dé and Gaillard, 20222;Le Dé, Wairama, Sath and Petera, 2021). Similarly, several others propose three categories: Index, score cards, and toolkits (Laurien, Martin and Mehryar, 2022;Cutter, 2016), while other methods used to measure resilience include indicator ranking, models, and simulations (Nashwan and Shahid, 2020). It is important to note that there are indeed overlaps in these different methods, and there are sometimes difficulties in assigning categories. In attempting to simplify the categories, Saja et al. (2019) identified three categories of measures as Index based approaches, score cards/ranking methods, and participatory toolkits/case studies.

Once the different categories of measures are used, there is need for evaluating the level of community resilience. There are several measures of resilience yet they are criticized for relying partly or fully on formative indicators that may be viewed as predictors (Cutter, 2016). This hinders the evaluation of factors that promote resilience because the same variables (e.g., level of social capital or social competence) may serve as both the measure of community resilience (indicators) and the factors potentially promoting it (predictors) (Lindberg and Swearingen, 2020;Rapaport, Hornik-Lurie, Cohen, Lahad, Leykin and Aharonson-Daniel, 2018). This challenge is compounded by the fact that when assessing resilience across locations and time, such measures reflect variability in factors potentially promoting resilience rather than variability in resilience (Saja, Goonetilleke, Teo and Ziyath, 2019). As such, due care should be taken when measuring community resilience to Fig. 4. A dynamic social innovation process model for creating host mining community resilience.

avoid the confusion caused by measuring predictors of resilience (Rapaport et al., 2018). It is recommended that classical test theory and reliability estimation be used as it is based on understanding constructs through their indicators (Bollen and Bauldry, 2011;Peterson, 2014;Lindberg and Swearingen, 2020). Lindberg and Swearingen (2020) identified two types of reflective measures which are: thrive-oriented reflective (effect) indicator (for example, Burton, 2015), and surveys (Gu, Dillard, Gerst and Loerzel, 2023). According to the Burton (2015) it was possible to assess the recovery of the built environment at a subcounty level, along the Mississippi Gulf Coast, after Hurricane Katrina, as a reference measure to validate an index of community resilience. However, this measure is criticised as it is limited to the available geography and evaluated changes (environmental, economic, or otherwise), based on previous occurrence of the changes and indicator measurements (Lindberg and Swearingen, 2020). Meanwhile, surveys or similar primary data collection methods are more robust as they rely on respondent perceptions and expectations, allowing assessment of community resilience using a reflective scale that is not limited by past occurrence of natural hazards or other changes, additionally capturing general and or specific resilience (Cénat et al., 2021;Lindberg and Swearingen, 2020).

Measuring and evaluating community resilience is an important way to learn from past experiences, allowing all actors to understand community needs and challenges in different ways. Choudhury et al. (2021) studied how transformative learning and actions of risk mitigation shape community resilience to climate-induced disasters. They carried out a mixed-method empirical investigation on the southern coast of Bangladesh and found the relationship between transformative learning and resilience-building to be complex, as it involves multiple social cultural-structural factors (such as, beliefs, values, power structures), practical considerations (including impact on livelihood, evacuation, and relocation logistics), and cognitive factors (Gu, Dillard, Gerst and Loerzel, 2023). It is argued that local culture significantly influences how people perceive and respond to risks. Although the role of learning is acknowledged, learning enhances resilience only when it leads to actionable steps. A finding that was surprising from the study was that relying solely on past experiences can create a false sense of security, making individuals believe future disasters will be similar. This is detrimental to effective preparedness. To mitigate climate-related disasters, it is essential to cultivate forward-thinking attitudes and adopt innovative strategies, such as social networking, which promotes social learning (Choudhury and Emdad Haque, 2018).

Notably, social learning has diverse meanings, applications, connotations, and acquisition processes involving individual, network, and system-centric approaches (Rodela 2011(Rodela , 2013)). When gleaned in the climate-induced disaster risk and resilience context, social learning can be considered a deliberate or spontaneous process wherein different stakeholders participate in a collective learning platform to share their experiences and opinions, learn from each other, and come to a common understanding of the issues that contribute to adaptive resilience (Cutter et al. 2008;Johannessen and Hahn 2013;Baird et al. 2014). What is critical to remember, though, is that social interactions and networks, important as they are, do not occur in a contextual vacuum divorced from local institutions. In mining communities in emerging markets, it would be critical to examine such a normative conceptualization of social learning by investigating how power-knowledge plays out within institutional contexts that in turn shape, access to local knowledge, social learning processes and resilience outcomes (Boyd et al. 2014;Ensor and Harvey 2015). Taking these arguments together, the following three propositions are suggested: Proposition 6. Social innovation impact assessment is strengthened when mining operations have a deep understanding of community needs and ecological crises unique to the host area.

Proposition 7. Social innovation benefits flowing to enhance the creation of community resilience are strengthened when mining operations engage in measuring and evaluating performance. Lessons stemming from mining operations' ability to gauge, reflect, and learn from different measures amplify community resilience. Proposition 8. Community resilience created from engaging with the community and other actors, provides a mining operation with important conditions for leveraging social innovation, through enhanced community attributes.

div.head: Practical implications for the mining industry in Southern Africa
div.p: This study has several implications for mining firms operating in Southern Africa communities characterised by high levels of unemployment, poverty, inequality, and poor socio-economic alternatives. Research has already shown that the impacts of climate change and biodiversity loss is unproportionately more severe in the Global South (countries that are economically less developed) and that with high inequality the communities are impacted with varying degrees. The mining firms, typically operating in the remote parts of Southern Africa would need to play an active role in creating resilient communities to mitigate the severity of climate change impacts.

Operations could invest in research and measurement to identify the unique ecological challenges in their operating ecosystems. A welldefined program of assessment will be pertinent, including baseline studies followed by monitoring, evaluation and drawing lessons from the activities and social innovations deployed. For example, Vedanta Resources limited with global operations, including in Southern Africa, has systematically designed mechanisms to measure and track their social performance (Vedanta, 2023). As part of these assessments, it is useful to pay attention to local indigenous knowledge so that traditional methods and cultural preservation are integrated into modern methods of handling climate change and biodiversity loss and mitigating their impacts. Implats, in South Africa and Zimbabwe, is constantly monitoring water, energy, community food systems, and biodiversity through crafted authorisation processes, management plans and standards (Impala Platinum, 2023). It is important to constantly measure community resilience and disaster preparedness as part of the needs and impact assessments of mining operations to provide early warning. The internet of things and Artificial Intelligence could play an important role in this approach.

Meaningful stakeholder engagement beyond the tick-box legal requirements entails engaging in inclusive dialogue with local communities. This helps mining operations to understand the needs, aspirations, fears, and challenges of communities to jointly come up with innovative solutions. There are opportunities to forge partnerships with local communities, government at different levels, NGOs, not-forprofit and other for-profit organisations in the mining host communities. Collaborations and stakeholder engagement will allow common understanding of social innovation dimensions including taking stock of the resources available in the communities and what needs to be brought in to build the much-needed resilience. These resources include infrastructure such as roads, health facilities, schools but also digital technology infrastructure for effective communication, capacity building and disaster management. Anglo American and Exxaro partnered with provincial governments and World Vision to solve the pressing challenges of climate change and biodiversity under the Impact Catalyst program (Impact Catalyst, 2023).

It is recommended that mining firms go beyond the traditional corporate social responsibility strategies aimed at simply building reputation through public relations. Committing to creating resilient communities by leveraging firm expertise and capacity to allow spillovers to communities presents companies with transformational opportunities in the era of climate change. In South Africa, African Rainbow Minerals innovatively partnered local communities to establish two Not-for-Profit Companies (NPCs) at their Modikwa Mine where periodic dividends are used by communities to build resilience through economic projects, health facilities and road infrastructure construction (ARM, 2023). However, studies have called for further investigation of the mechanisms to enhance the effectiveness of such community initiatives (Phasha, 2020;Gilberthorpe, 2015;Tawaziwa and Wedzerai, 2014). Partnerships with academic institutions for further development of these solutions could provide useful lessons and models.

Social performance initiatives could be more deliberately designed with climate change in mind. When organisations focus on biodiversity and climate adaptation strategies, it is important to involve communities as joint implementers of programs. This helps in building the capacity of communities for resilience beyond the life of the mine. For example, ICMM reports an emphasis on nature-based solutions in ecosystems where their members operate (ICMM, 2024). The current efforts to decarbonise mining firms need to cascade to the supply chains and into communities if the world is to tackle the devastating impacts of global warming. For example, local enterprise development and local content initiatives could integrate ecological resilience to build local economic capacity and ecologically sensitive behaviour beyond the life of the mine. As organisations embrace environmental stewardship initiatives, such as land rehabilitation, reforestation and water management, it is important to ensure these efforts are also embraced by communities. A typical example of this initiative is Rio Tinto Richards Bay Minerals in South Africa, which mines sand dunes along the coast while deploying progressive dune rehabilitation. The company has been learning and sharing lessons with local and international communities (Rio Tinto, 2024). Once minerals are removed from the sand, the dunes are reshaped back as close as possible to their pre-mining topography, with topsoil rich in indigenous vegetation seeds and organic matter spread over the reshaped dunes and enriched with fast-growing annuals to begin biological processes and to protect the topsoil from wind and water erosion, fostering biodiversity while greening and stabilising the dunes (Dlamini and Xulu, 2019;Ott, 2017;van Aarde, Ferreira, Kritzinger, Van Dyk, Vogt and Wassenaar, 1996).

Training that is tailor made to address ecological crises in host communities and keep records and learnings to address future crises is on the rise. This is also an area where collaboration with other stakeholders, including universities and non-governmental organisation will be useful. In South Africa, for example, African Rainbow Minerals collaborates with universities to address climate crises and in Limpopo province (ARM, 2023). Deliberate efforts to mitigate ecological crises, tackle social challenges, promote local economic development and protect the environment help mining organisations to build resilient communities. Such initiatives also reinforce their social licence to operate. This, however, is only possible when mining firms approach these efforts with long-term perspective and genuine commitment to well-being and empowerment of the communities, they operate in.

div.head: Conclusion and future research directions
div.p: Climate change and biodiversity loss have emerged as significant challenges in Southern Africa. The mining industry is expected to play a significant role in building capacity to mitigate the impacts of climate change and biodiversity loss in the communities in which they operate. This paper scopes the social innovation literature and explores opportunities for social innovation in building resilient communities in the face of the growing ecological dual crises.

We find that social innovation can enhance community resilience when specific conditions are met. An important consideration is thorough conceptualisation of what social innovation and community resilience mean in the context of sustainable development in emerging markets. It is necessary to conceptualise social innovation as new socially centred processes, practices, technologies, or combinations of these for improved results. It is argued that mining companies may benefit from understanding the needs of and challenges faced by communities for social innovation to have a remarkable effect on community resilience.

The paper identifies resources, capabilities and constraints, governance, networks and actors, and process dynamism as important dimensions of social innovation when the aim is to create community resilience in mining local ecosystems. For sustainable resilience to be achieved, important community attributes are community active agency, absorptive capacity to draw lessons and culture. For that reason, mining operations will need to actively engage with communities and other actors, draw from resources and capabilities, adjust governance mechanisms, and respond to process dynamics to create resilient communities in the face of ecological crises.

Measuring and evaluating community resilience reflectively to understand the level of economic development, social capital, community capacity, and information and communication capacity is important for learning to strengthen the social innovation benefits flowing to the community. Reflective measuring is important to avoid measuring the predictors of community resilience but the indicators.

Future studies could build on propositions outlined for quantitative measurement to test the theoretical framework. A mixed methods approach could be used in such studies for researchers to capture the dynamic nature of the proposed processes in creating community resilience. We also suggest that future studies could draw from mining operations cited as examples in this paper to investigate and quantitatively test the theory.

Another important avenue for future research will be to consider how social innovation could be integrated into other theories widely used in mining-community research, such as stakeholder theory, corporate social responsibility frameworks, social and environmental impact assessment, and social licence to operate. These are areas with a large body of literature which could be useful in theorising social innovation specifically for the mining industry. Although this paper highlights the importance of a broad definition of social innovation to include technological innovation with a societal focus, we see an opportunity for exploring how digital transformation specifically plays a role in social innovation as a mechanism for community resilience. This is especially relevant because an important dimension of community resilience identified in this research in information and communication.

For emerging markets with limited information and capacity for communication technology, it will be important to understand how social innovation could advance that area. Closely linked to technological transformation in mining is the role of social innovation in addressing inequality and gender issues for sustainable resilience that is enhanced by technology, inclusive, and diverse. This is important as our study finds that community resilience is not achieved by the resilience of individuals but a combined, collaborative adaptability of communities to shocks.
